evidence.label: Virtual compact specialness of hyperbolic one-relator groups

headline: Claims one-relator groups without Baumslag–Solitar subgroups are hyperbolic, and hyperbolic ones are virtually compact special.
scope: Finitely generated groups with one defining relation. Two companion papers; neither has a Lean formalization.
plain: A one-relator group is built from free generators and a single rule. Some such groups contain special pieces called Baumslag–Solitar groups, which stretch distances badly. Gersten conjectured these are the only thing stopping hyperbolicity, a large-scale negative curvature. The first paper claims to prove this. The second claims every hyperbolic one-relator group has a finite cover with a strong cube geometry.
doesNot: This does not have a Lean formalization, and it does not cover groups with more than one defining relation.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Steve Gersten, who asked whether Baumslag–Solitar subgroups are the only obstructions
scorecard.significanceWhy: Gersten's conjecture and the cubulation of hyperbolic one-relator groups are central open problems for one-relator groups.

explanation:
Take two generators a and t with one rule: t a t⁻¹ = a². This is the Baumslag–Solitar group BS(1, 2). Apply the rule twice: t² a t⁻² = t a² t⁻¹ = a⁴. After k steps, t^k a t^−k = a^(2^k). For k = 10 that gives a¹⁰²⁴. The left side has only 10 + 1 + 10 = 21 letters. So a power of a that seems 1024 letters long has a 21-letter shortcut. Such exponential shortcuts cannot happen in a hyperbolic group.

A one-relator group has finitely many generators and one defining rule. BS(m, n) is the group with rule t a^m t⁻¹ = a^n, for nonzero m and n[1]. These groups are the basic obstructions to hyperbolicity among one-relator groups[1]. A word-hyperbolic group is one whose distance graph has thin triangles. The flat grid Z² is BS(1, 1), with rule t a t⁻¹ = a, so the conjecture excludes it too[2]. Gersten asked whether Baumslag–Solitar subgroups are the only obstructions[3].

Partial answers came from the hierarchy method. Magnus showed in 1930 that dropping a generator from the rule leaves a free subgroup[4]. Newman's spelling theorem gave hyperbolicity for relators that are proper powers[5]. Linton showed a one-relator group is hyperbolic and locally quasiconvex exactly when its primitivity rank is not two[6]. The obstacle was hyperbolicity alone in the primitivity-rank-two case. There the splittings need not stay geometrically controlled.

The first paper claims the full conjecture. If a one-relator group contains no BS(m, n) subgroup, then it is word-hyperbolic[7]. The proof uses Magnus splittings and a combination theorem, which gives hyperbolicity when annuli in a graph of groups flare out[8].

The second paper claims that every hyperbolic one-relator group is virtually compact special[9]. That means a finite-index subgroup is the loop group of a finite cube complex. That complex maps nicely to the model space of a right-angled Artin group. A right-angled Artin group has one generator per vertex of a graph, with commuting rules along edges. This structure implies residual finiteness: every nonidentity element survives in some finite quotient[10]. Combined with work of Kielak and Linton, it answers Wise's question: hyperbolic one-relator groups are virtually free-by-cyclic[11].

How sure is this? Neither paper has a Lean formalization. No specialist review of either paper has been published. These are claims by the papers, not checked results.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Neither paper has a Lean formalization or a published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A group with finitely many generators and a single defining rule.
The group BS(m, n) with generators a and t and the one rule t a^m t⁻¹ = a^n.
A finitely generated group whose distance graph has uniformly thin triangles.
The least rank of a free subgroup containing the relator where the relator is not part of a free basis.
A finite-index subgroup is the loop group of a finite cube complex that maps locally isometrically to a right-angled Artin model.
Every nonidentity element stays nonidentity in some finite image of the group.
An extension of a free group by a subgroup of the integers.
